I put c11 in `final.py`. Its search score is **81.0** (the reference scores about 1.0), and I used **5 of the 24 scorer calls**. The search took about 7 minutes of the 15 I'd planned; I stopped early because the last few changes were too small to measure.

| | search score | CPU time on scorer |
|---|---|---|
| baseline | ~1.0 | 1.32 s |
| first champion (c1) | 68.5 | 19.3 ms |
| c5 | 75.3 | 17.5 ms |
| c7 | 78.8 | 16.6 ms |
| c9 | 81.3 | 16.4 ms |
| **final (c11)** | **81.0** | 16.3 ms |

There's no held-out split I can score, so the held-out check was done on my own harness instead. On instance seeds I never tuned on (5–8), `final.py` was correct and 40–53× faster than the reference. It also matched the reference exactly on about 300 small edge-case inputs (empty and whitespace-only records, case differences, repeated words, exact duplicates) and on stress inputs: a tiny vocabulary, long records, heavy duplication and near-misses.

**Why it's faster:** the reference compares every pair of records. `final.py` compares only pairs that could possibly reach 80 %:
- **Identical word sets are grouped first.** They pair with each other directly, and each group is checked only once.
- **Words are ranked from rarest to most common.** Each set only needs its first few words in that order checked against an index (`n − ⌈0.8n⌉ + 1` words). Two sets that are 80 % alike must share one of those words, so this never misses a pair.
- **Sets are processed from smallest to largest.** Candidates more than 20 % smaller are skipped without being compared.
- **Small sets skip the search.** Two different sets of 4 words or fewer can never be 80 % alike, so those sets are only indexed.
- **Words that appear in only one set are ignored**, since they can't be shared.
- **No imports.** Leaving out `collections` saved about 1 ms of import time, which is counted in the score.
- **Long sets are compared as bit masks.** For sets of 12 or more words, the shared words are counted on integers instead of by set intersection. This only applies when fewer than 8,192 words are shared across records; above that, masks would get slow. It made no difference on the search split, but it was 5–7× faster on inputs with long records, where the previous version was only 1.9× faster than the reference.

**Other approaches tried:**
- Ordering words alphabetically instead of by rarity was about 16× slower than rarity order, so I dropped it.
- Bit masks are kept for long sets only, as above.
- Fast paths and lookup tables for small sets (c7–c9) gave small gains.

Most of the remaining time is now spent splitting each record into words, so further changes gain little.

**Candidate log** (calls left: 19):
- c1, first champion: 68.5. Kept.
- c2, shorter index entries plus integer ranks: 16 % faster on the harness. Kept.
- c3, small micro-optimisations: no change. Dropped.
- c4, alphabetical order: 16× slower. Dropped.
- c5, no imports: 75.3. Kept.
- c6, building the word sets with `map`: no change. Dropped.
- c7, skipping single-use words plus lookup tables: 78.8. Kept.
- c8/c9, small-set fast path: 81.3. Kept.
- c10/c11, bit masks for long sets with the vocabulary guard: 81.0, tied with c9 but more robust. **Final.**
- c12, counting words while grouping: no change. Dropped.

All my files are in `work/` inside the task folder. `work/harness.py` checks correctness against the reference and times candidates; `work/bench.py` compares timings.
